source.title: Truthfulness Despite Weak Supervision: Evaluating and Training LLMs Using Peer Prediction
source.authors: Tianyi Qiu; Micah Carroll; Cameron S. Allen

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports peer-prediction-based truthfulness training with a weak expert, but does not test the weak-to-strong intervention or any of the specified claim versions: it does not train a strong student on labels from a weak supervisor and compare the student with that supervisor or report PGR.
record.gate_note: The reported recovery from deceptive fine-tuning is a related result about training with a weak peer-prediction reward, not the weak-supervisor-label comparison in the claim. The paper's deception-evaluation and domain-correlation results do not measure a listed version. The text says peer-prediction training recovers most of the accuracy drop and outperforms LLM-as-a-Judge with a 7B judge; it does not give those training results as exact numerical values in text.
record.test_reason: No version is tested. The study never fine-tunes a strong student on a weak model's labels, never compares the student with the weak supervisor or a strong ceiling, and reports no PGR. Its training result uses peer-prediction scores from a 135M expert as a DPO preference signal, built from other 8B participants' answers, to undo deliberately induced deception. Its other results concern evaluation: detecting deceptive answers. It does not cite the original weak-to-strong paper; it only discusses 'weak supervision' in the scalable-oversight sense.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as far as it goes, but incomplete. The authors also conclude that peer prediction is incentive compatible and resists deception without a stronger judge. On evaluation, they report an inverse-scaling property: resistance to deception grows with the expert–participant capability gap, and with the number of participants and experts.
record.recipe_differences: Uses peer-prediction scores as a DPO reward signal after deceptive finetuning, rather than fine-tuning a strong student on a weak model's labels and measuring PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that deception resistance varies with capability gap, participant population size, number of experts, and domain; these are evaluation results, not measurements of the listed weak-to-strong versions.

fits_no_version.finding: Peer-prediction DPO with a SmolLM-135M expert recovers most of the accuracy lost when Llama-3.1-8B is fine-tuned to deceive. It beats LLM-as-a-Judge rewards from 135M or 7B judges (Figure 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A weak expert's peer-prediction reward can restore much of the truthfulness a stronger model lost to deceptive fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Inverse scaling: peer-prediction resistance to deception improves as the participant-to-expert size ratio grows, up to over 100x. LLM-as-a-Judge falls below random against deceptive models 5–20x the judge's size (Figure 2, Figure 10, Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak evaluators detect a stronger model's deception better, not worse, as the capability gap widens under peer prediction.

record.problems: The relevant truthfulness-training result is described qualitatively in the text; exact plotted accuracies and uncertainty for that result are not given there. The experiment uses prompt-induced deceptive training and does not compare the trained model against the weak expert as a supervisor.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded peer-prediction deception-detection and evaluation results, including scaling and cross-domain analyses, because they do not measure any listed weak-to-strong version or the training outcome represented by R1.

untested.parts: All of it: no student trained on weak-model labels, no weak-supervisor comparison, no strong ceiling, no PGR.
All of it: no auxiliary confidence loss, weak-supervisor ensembles or loss variants against naive weak-label fine-tuning. The expert-ensemble results concern deception detection, not PGR.
All of it: the capability-gap scaling concerns deception-detection loss, not PGR across supervisor and student sizes.
All of it: deception is induced on purpose by prompts, LoRA training or MisleadLM; this is not a strong student exploiting a weak supervisor's labels.
All of it: the theorems give incentive compatibility of peer prediction, not conditions under which a student must beat its supervisor.
All of it: no vision experiments.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels, because no version is tested. The training experiment uses four 8B participants, one prompted to deceive, and a 135M expert used only as a scorer. The 'weak supervision' framing overlaps in spirit with weak-to-strong, but the measured quantities (ground-truth accuracy recovery, honesty-prediction cross-entropy) are not PGR or a student-versus-supervisor comparison. Relation could arguably be cites_only or discusses; 'discusses' is kept.

versions.untested_parts: No weak-to-strong training on weak-model labels, comparison with the weak supervisor, or PGR.
Does not compare the listed training changes with naive weak-label fine-tuning or report PGR.
No PGR analysis across supervisor/student sizes, tasks, or representations.
Deception experiments concern peer-prediction evaluation and deliberately induced deceptive participants, not the listed weak-to-strong failure modes.
The theory concerns incentive compatibility of peer prediction, not conditions requiring a student to beat its supervisor.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B (deceptively trained model)
rows.stage_stated: instruction-tuned; LoRA-finetuned for deception, then LoRA DPO
rows.operation_detail: LoRA DPO on 120k paired answers selected for high versus low peer-prediction score

conditions.value: LoRA finetuning on 50k model-generated deceptive answers

rows.measure: Ground-truth accuracy recovery after deceptive training
rows.baseline: Accuracy after deceptive training; exact value not stated in the text
rows.value: The authors state that most of the accuracy drop from deception training is recovered; peer-prediction training with the 0.135B expert outperforms LLM-as-a-Judge training with a 7B judge.
rows.note: Related weak-expert reward-training result, not a weak-to-strong labels experiment; no comparison with the weak expert's task performance and no PGR. The figure plots accuracy by training step, but exact values are not stated in the accompanying text.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked; this is a related weak-reward training result, not weak-to-strong label training. The baseline is not fully unstated: Figure 1's data labels show the original model at 50.80%, deceptive training as low as about 34.2–34.4%, and the best recovered points about 47.7–47.9%. The curve-to-label mapping is inferred from the figure text, so the values are approximate. 'Partial' describes incomplete recovery toward the original model, not a state on any claim version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
